title: Index funds: tracking the market
subtitle: Index funds
openingQuestion: What does an index fund tracking VN30 do when the Index Committee changes VN30's composition (removes one stock, adds another)?
openingOptions: The fund manager holds a careful meeting and subjectively decides whether to follow that change or not
The fund automatically adjusts its portfolio to match the new composition, with no analysis or forecasting needed
The fund keeps its old portfolio exactly as originally committed to investors, regardless of how the reference index changes
The fund is forced to close entirely and return all principal to investors as soon as the basket's composition changes
explanation: The essence of an index fund is to precisely replicate a benchmark index - with no subjective opinion. When the index changes its composition, the fund automatically buys/sells to keep its portfolio matched to the index - this is a mechanical process, not based on human judgment.

diagram.label: The index fund automatically buys/sells to match
The portfolio always matches the index

realWorldExample.company: Open-ended funds like SSI-SCA or VNDAF tracking index baskets
realWorldExample.description: Many fund managers in Vietnam (SSI Asset Management, VinaCapital, Dragon Capital...) run index funds mimicking VN30 or VNDiamond. When HOSE announces the new VN30 list every 6 months (usually removing stocks that no longer meet liquidity/cap standards and adding new ones), these funds automatically rebalance their portfolios accordingly, with no analyst team needed to decide which stock to pick.

quiz.question: What is the goal of an index fund?
options: Concentrate all capital in the most promising stock
Actively pick the best stocks to beat the market
Maximize dividends received each year regardless of risk, the defining feature of this fund type
Replicate the performance of a benchmark index as closely as possible
quiz.explanation: An index fund doesn't try to pick 'better than the market' stocks. Its sole goal is to track the benchmark index's performance as closely as possible, accepting a return equal to the market average instead of trying to outperform.

quiz.question: Why do index funds usually have much lower management fees than active funds?
options: Because it's a mechanical replication, needing no research team
Because index funds are banned from charging management fees to investors
Because index funds don't have to comply with fund management regulations
Because index funds can only invest in a single stock
quiz.explanation: An index fund doesn't need an expensive team of experts researching, analyzing and picking stocks - its job is just to precisely replicate an existing index by formula. This sharply reduces operating costs compared to an active fund.

quiz.question: The VN30 index changes its composition, removing one stock and adding another. What does a VN30 index fund do?
options: Keep the old portfolio unchanged since the index change doesn't force the fund to follow
Automatically sell the removed ticker and buy the new one
Convene an investment committee to decide whether to buy the new ticker
Sell the entire portfolio into cash and wait for the index to stabilize
quiz.explanation: This is exactly the core difference: an index fund has no opinion of its own. If the index changes composition, the fund changes with it, even if the manager personally thinks the new ticker is expensive or the old one still good. Mechanical sounds like a drawback, but it removes exactly the thing that harms investors most: emotional judgment.

quiz.question: What does an index fund's tracking error tell you?
options: The number of times the fund placed a wrong order in the year and had to cancel and redo it
The proportion of stocks in the fund's portfolio delisted during the reporting period
The gap between the fund's performance and the performance of the index it tracks
The excess return the fund earns over the index by timing purchases and sales well
quiz.explanation: An index fund tries to replicate the index but never matches it perfectly: management fees, cash held as a buffer for redemptions, and the lag when rebalancing all create a deviation. A low tracking error is a sign of good execution - for an index fund, tracking closely is the success, not outperforming.

quiz.question: Why can an index fund still lose money even though it 'only mimics the market'?
options: Because an index fund only replicates the index's upside, not its downside
Because the annual management fee is always larger than the benchmark index's return which nobody could reasonably deny
Because the fund must sell stock at low prices whenever investors redeem
Because when the whole market falls, the index falls and the fund falls right along with it
quiz.explanation: Mimicking the market means following it in both directions. Diversification erases the risk of any single company, but it doesn't erase the risk of the entire market - in 2022 the VN-Index fell over 30% and every VN30 index fund fell along with it.

quiz.question: A 25-year-old investor plans to contribute evenly each month for 20 years. Why is an index fund usually recommended for this case?
options: Because fees are low and it doesn't depend on picking the right fund manager
Because an index fund guarantees a minimum return for periodic monthly contributions
Because an index fund waives all trading fees for investors who contribute monthly
Because over 20 years an index fund is guaranteed to outperform every active fund
quiz.explanation: Over a long horizon, the two things that erode results the most are fees and picking the wrong fund. An index fund handles both: much lower fees, and you don't have to bet that today's skilled manager will still be there 20 years from now.

keyTakeaways: An index fund replicates the performance of a benchmark index (VN30, S&P 500...), not trying to select stocks to beat the market
Portfolio rebalancing happens automatically by formula, not based on human subjective judgment
Index fund management fees are usually much lower than active funds thanks to not needing an expensive research team

practicePrompt.question: You're comparing 2 funds that both track the VN30 index. Fund A has no research team, only replicates the VN30 basket weighting exactly. Fund B claims to have experts who 'fine-tune' the portfolio to outperform the index. Which one is a true index fund?
options: Fund A, since a true index fund mechanically replicates the benchmark rather than trying to beat it
Fund B, because having an expert analyst team always means the fund operates as a true index fund model
Both are equally index funds, because both track the same benchmark index VN30 in their name
Neither is a true index fund, because every investment fund in Vietnam is required to have its own analyst team
practicePrompt.explanation: Fund B with experts who 'fine-tune' to beat the index is actually an active fund, not an index fund - even if it names itself after the benchmark index.

summary.keyIdea: An index fund replicates the performance of a benchmark index (VN30, S&P 500...), not trying to select stocks to beat the market
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: Portfolio rebalancing happens automatically by formula, not based on human subjective judgment

application.title: Read a fund's fact sheet
application.message: The lesson already has a real example with E1VFVN30's factsheet figures (management fee, expense ratio, rebalancing frequency) - see the 'Real example' section above. Now try applying those same 4 items to another index fund you're interested in.
application.secondary: Reading a real factsheet once helps you feel much more confident choosing a fund later on.

sections.text: An index fund sounds like a complicated concept, but its philosophy is actually extremely simple: instead of trying to guess which stock will win, an index fund accepts buying exactly what the market currently has, in exactly the weighting the market has decided.

An index is a number representing the average performance of a group of stocks. The VN-Index represents the entire HOSE exchange, VN30 represents the 30 largest-cap stocks. An index fund is designed to precisely replicate the movement of a specific index - if VN30 rises 10% in the year, an index fund tracking VN30 will also rise close to 10% (minus a small management fee).
How it works: mechanical, not emotional

The core difference of an index fund versus other forms of investing is that it has no subjective opinion. The fund manager doesn't sit and analyze which stock is 'good' or 'bad' - their job is only to ensure the fund's portfolio always matches the benchmark index's weighting. When the index-operating body (like HOSE with VN30) announces basket-composition changes every 6 months, the fund automatically buys the newly added stocks and sells the removed ones.

items: An index fund doesn't try to 'beat the market' - the goal is to track the market's average performance
The portfolio is rebalanced automatically by formula, not depending on the manager's emotions or judgment
Operating costs are low since no research team is needed to analyze each stock
The index fund's risk is nearly identical to the overall risk of the market it tracks

sections.label: Why many experts recommend beginners start with index funds
sections.text: Long-term research shows that most active funds (managed by experts picking stocks) don't outperform their benchmark index after fees, especially over 10-20 years. This makes index funds a sensible choice for those without the time or deep expertise to pick their own stocks.
How does an index fund differ from an ETF?

This is a point many people confuse. 'Index fund' is an investment philosophy (replicating an index), while ETF is a specific packaging and trading format (a fund certificate traded on the exchange like a stock). Most popular ETFs are index funds, but an index fund can also exist as a traditional open-ended fund (bought/sold through a fund manager, not traded in real time on an exchange like an ETF).
A real example: reading E1VFVN30's factsheet

Instead of just theory, let's look at a real factsheet. E1VFVN30 (the DCVFMVN30 ETF, managed by Dragon Capital) is Vietnam's largest domestic ETF tracking VN30 - its factsheet usually discloses the following items, and these are E1VFVN30's real figures for you to compare against:

items: Benchmark: VN30 - the fund commits to replicating the exact weighting of the 30 stocks in this basket, not picking other stocks
Management fee: 0.65%/year on NAV - this is the only fee the fund charges to operate, much lower than the 1.5-2%/year common at active funds

Total expense ratio: about 0.9%/year - includes the management fee plus other operating costs (custody, audit, trading...); this is the most important figure to compare between funds because it reflects the actual cost you pay

Rebalancing frequency: every 6 months, matching HOSE's schedule for reviewing the VN30 basket (changed in January and July each year) - the fund doesn't decide this timing itself, it follows the index's schedule exactly

sections.label: How to apply this when reading another fund's factsheet
sections.text: Open the factsheet (usually a 1-2 page PDF, published publicly by the fund manager's website), find these same 4 items: which index the fund tracks, the management fee %/year, the total expense ratio %, and the rebalancing frequency. Comparing the expense ratio between 2-3 funds tracking the same index is the fastest way to pick the cheaper fund without sacrificing anything on performance, since index funds with the same benchmark have nearly identical performance.

lines: An index fund replicates a benchmark index by mechanical formula, not trying to guess which stock will win.
Low cost and market-tracking performance make this a solid starting choice for a beginning long-term investor.
